# Imaging

Rasters and computer vision: convolution and the filter family, gradients and edges, corners, blobs and morphology, multiscale pyramids, warps and optical flow. Dependency-free CPU float math built on one value type, `Img`, with the separable-convolution core vectorized to roughly OpenCV's single-threaded speed. Every detector hands back geometry, so results go straight to `lines()`.

6 source file(s), 255 public symbol(s), 209 of them carrying KDoc. Everything below is the documentation that lives beside the code — the same text the [completion documentation panel](../completion_doc_browser.md) shows in the editor. ## imaging.kt { #imaging-kt }

CPU image / computer-vision family for the Field stdlib — the raster counterpart to the
time-domain `timeseries.kt` and frequency-domain `spectral.kt` families.

Field's stated target domains include computer vision, but until now the stdlib had no image
layer at all: no convolution, no gradients, no pyramids, no features, no warps. This file (plus
`imaging_filters.kt`, `imaging_features.kt`, `imaging_geometry.kt`, `imaging_field.kt`) closes
that gap with a small, honest, dependency-free core.

The whole family is built on one value type, [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img):

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val photo  = imgFromFile("cat.png")        // 3-channel sRGB-ish floats in 0..1
val gray   = photo.luma()                  // 1 channel
val edges  = gray.sobelMagnitude()         // 1 channel
val canny  = gray.canny(0.08, 0.20)        // 1 channel binary mask
canny.toFLines()                           // .. straight into Field's drawing layer
```

Design choices, all deliberate:

- **Float channels, not bytes.** Every operation is float math in `0..1` (or unbounded, for
  gradients and Laplacians, which legitimately go negative). Nothing quantises mid-pipeline, so
  a 12-stage chain does not accumulate rounding steps. Clamping happens once, on output.
- **Immutable-by-convention value type.** Ops return a new [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img); the backing `FloatArray` is
  public (`data`) so a hot inner loop in a box can write it directly if it wants to.
  Interleaved channel-major-last layout (`data[(y*width + x)*channels + c]`), the same layout
  `BufferedImage`/GL/Vulkan uploads want.
- **1, 3 or 4 channels.** 1 = scalar/gray/mask, 3 = RGB, 4 = RGBA. Nothing else; a "12-channel
  feature tensor" is a different (and non-existent) problem.
- **No external dependency.** Pure Kotlin plus `javax.imageio` for load/save and
  `afield.util.PngEncoder` for the AWT-free path used by box output.
- **Live-codeable.** [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) implements [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so evaluating an `Img` in a box (or `img.h`)
  shows the actual picture as an inline thumbnail, not `Img@3f1a2b`.

Out of scope on purpose: GPU work (that is `afield.four` / StackSL / RectSL), video decoding,
and anything needing a model file.

## imaging_features.kt { #imaging-features-kt }

Edges, corners, lines, blobs and morphology for [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) — the "find things in the picture" half of
the stdlib imaging family (see `imaging.kt` for the value type and `imaging_filters.kt` for
convolution and gradients).

Everything here reduces pixels to *structure* — a point set, a label map, a list of lines — and
that structure is what `imaging_field.kt` turns into `FLine`s so it lands in Field's drawing
layer rather than staying trapped in a raster.

Every detector here is the textbook algorithm, implemented plainly and documented with the
property a test can check:

| function | what it finds | test invariant |
|---|---|---|
| `canny` | thin, connected edges | a synthetic square yields a 1-pixel-wide closed outline |
| `harrisCorners` / `shiTomasiCorners` | corners via the structure tensor | 4 responses at a square's 4 corners |
| `fastCorners` | corners via a brightness circle test | same, and much faster |
| `houghLines` | straight lines in polar form | a drawn line is recovered at its `(rho, theta)` |
| `connectedComponents` | blobs in a binary mask | N drawn discs give N labels with the right areas |
| `distanceTransform` | distance to the nearest zero | a disc's centre has distance = its radius |

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/imaging_features.kt`

**Used in:** [Imaging and computer vision](../imaging_examples.md), [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md)

The default tracker seed. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">fastCorners</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">threshold</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.08</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">contiguous</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">9</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">minDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">5</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">maxCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">300</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Corner</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | FAST corner detection (Rosten & Drummond): a pixel is a corner if at least `contiguous` of the 16 pixels on a radius-3 circle around it are all brighter than `centre + t` or all darker than `centre - t`. No gradients, no eigenvalues — just a wrap-around run-length test, which is why it is the fastest usable corner detector. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">houghLines</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">edges</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">thetaSteps</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">360</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">rhoStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">threshold</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">maxLines</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">20</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">minSeparationTheta</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.15</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">minSeparationRho</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">12.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">HoughLine</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Standard Hough line transform over a binary edge mask. |

Each edge pixel votes for the centres of all circles of each candidate radius passing through it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">erode</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">SQUARE</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Grayscale erosion: each pixel becomes the **minimum** over the structuring element. On a binary mask this shrinks bright regions and deletes anything thinner than the element. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">dilate</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">SQUARE</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Grayscale dilation: each pixel becomes the **maximum** over the structuring element. On a binary mask this grows bright regions and bridges gaps narrower than the element. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="k">open</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">SQUARE</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Erode then dilate — removes specks and thin protrusions, keeps the overall size of what remains. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">close</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">SQUARE</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Dilate then erode — fills pinholes and hairline cracks, keeps the overall size. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">morphologicalGradient</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">SQUARE</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | `dilate - erode`: a one-pixel-ish outline of every bright region. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">topHat</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">3</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">SQUARE</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | `image - open(image)`: bright detail smaller than the element (specks, text on a gradient). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">blackHat</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">3</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">shape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">StructuringElement</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">SQUARE</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | `close(image) - image`: dark detail smaller than the element. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">connectedComponents</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">connectivity</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">8</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ComponentLabelling</span></code> | Two-pass connected-component labelling of a binary mask (samples > 0.5 are foreground), with per-blob area, bounding box and centroid. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">distanceTransform</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Euclidean distance transform of a binary mask: each foreground pixel's value becomes its distance (in pixels) to the nearest background pixel. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">traceContours</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">minPerimeter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">8</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Trace the outline of every blob in a binary mask as a closed pixel-boundary polygon (Moore-neighbour tracing). ## imaging_field.kt { #imaging-field-kt }

What makes the imaging family *Field's* rather than a generic CV library: the bridges out of the
raster and into the things Field already draws, colours and displays.

Three bridges:

 1. **Structure → `FLine`.** Every detector in `imaging_features.kt` produces geometry, and
    geometry in Field is an `FLine`. `Img.toContourFLines`, `cornersToFLines`, `linesToFLines`,
    `FlowField.toFLines` and `Img.isoContourFLines` hand you drawable lines, so a Canny result
    goes straight into the same drawing/animation/export machinery as anything hand-drawn.
 2. **Scalar → colour.** `Img.colormap` runs a 1-channel response image through the same
    [`Colormaps`](visualization.md#colormaps-kt-colormaps) tables RectSL's `heat`/`bars`/`scatter` use, so a Harris response, a distance
    transform and a RectSL chart are coloured by one source of truth.
 3. **Value → screen.** [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) is a [`afield.ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so evaluating one in a box shows the picture;
    `Box.showImg` pushes a full-size version to an output channel, and `Box.showImgGrid` lays
    several out side by side with captions — the fastest way to see a whole pipeline at once.

The scalar-field bridge runs the other way too: `Img.asScalarField2D` adapts an [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) to the
`ScalarField2D` type `contours.kt` marches, so Field's existing marching-squares iso-contour
extractor works on image data with no glue.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/imaging_field.kt`

**Used in:** [Imaging and computer vision](../imaging_examples.md), [Wave Function Collapse examples](../wfc_examples.md), [Spatial artificial life](../alife_examples.md)

## imaging_filters.kt { #imaging-filters-kt }

Convolution, smoothing, gradients and multiscale pyramids for [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) — the filter half of the
stdlib imaging family (see `imaging.kt` for the value type, `imaging_features.kt` for edges,
corners and blobs).

Everything here is per-channel: a 3-channel image blurs each of R, G, B independently. Filters
that only make sense on a scalar field (`sobel`, `laplacian`, …) take the `Img.luma` of a colour
input automatically rather than erroring, because that is what you meant.

Two performance-relevant choices worth knowing about:

- **Separable when possible.** Gaussian and box blurs run as two 1-D passes (`O(k)` per pixel,
  not `O(k²)`). `convolveSeparable` is public so your own separable kernels get the same
  treatment, and `convolve2D` exists both as a general fallback and as the naive reference the
  unit tests check the separable path against.
- **Box blur is a running sum.** `boxBlur` is `O(1)` per pixel regardless of radius, so a
  radius-40 mean is as cheap as radius-1. Three box passes approximate a Gaussian closely
  (see `boxBlurApproxGaussian`) if you need a very large sigma cheaply.

**Used in:** [Imaging and computer vision](../imaging_examples.md), [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md)

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">correlate2D</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">k</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Kernel2D</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Cross-correlation with `k` (kernel *not* flipped). This is what most "apply this stencil" intuitions actually mean; identical to `convolve2D` for symmetric kernels. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">gaussianBlur</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">truncate</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">4.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Gaussian blur with standard deviation `sigma`, run as two separable 1-D passes. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">boxBlur</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Box (mean) blur over a `(2*radius+1)²` window, computed with running sums so the cost is independent of `radius`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">boxBlurApproxGaussian</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Three successive `boxBlur` passes, which by the central limit theorem approximate a Gaussian of standard deviation `sigma` — `O(1)` per pixel at any sigma. Use when sigma is large and you care more about speed than about the exact kernel shape. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">median</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">radius</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Median filter over a `(2*radius+1)²` window — the standard salt-and-pepper de-noiser, and unlike a mean it does not smear edges. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">bilateral</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigmaSpace</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">3.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sigmaRange</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.1</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Bilateral filter: a Gaussian blur whose weights are additionally attenuated by intensity distance, so it smooths flat regions while leaving edges sharp. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">unsharpMask</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.5</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">amount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">threshold</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Unsharp mask: `image + amount * (image - gaussianBlur(image, sigma))`. The oldest sharpening trick there is; `threshold` suppresses amplification of low-contrast noise. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sobel</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Gradient</span></code> | Sobel gradients. The 3x3 Sobel operator factors into a `[-1, 0, 1]` derivative across the gradient axis and a `[1, 2, 1]/4` smoothing along it, so both components run separably. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">sobelMagnitude</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Shorthand for `sobel().magnitude()`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">scharr</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Gradient</span></code> | Scharr gradients — same structure as `sobel` but with the `[3, 10, 3]/16` smoothing factor, which has markedly better rotational symmetry (the direction estimate is more accurate on diagonal edges). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">gaussianGradient</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">truncate</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">4.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Gradient</span></code> | Gradients of a Gaussian-smoothed image at scale `sigma`, computed as the analytic derivative of the Gaussian (not a blur followed by a difference), so the scale is exact. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">laplacian</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">eightNeighbour</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Discrete Laplacian (second derivative). `eightNeighbour` picks `LAPLACIAN_8` over `LAPLACIAN_4`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">laplacianOfGaussian</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.5</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Laplacian of Gaussian at scale `sigma` — computed as the difference of the image and its blur's Laplacian, i.e. `laplacian(gaussianBlur(img, sigma))`. Zero crossings are edges at that scale. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">differenceOfGaussians</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigma1</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sigma2</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">2.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">border</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Border</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Border</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">CLAMP</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | Difference of Gaussians, `blur(sigma1) - blur(sigma2)` with `sigma1 < sigma2` — the cheap band-pass approximation to `laplacianOfGaussian` and the basis of blob detection. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">pyrDown</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | One-octave downsample: blur by `sigma` then take every other pixel. The blur is what keeps this from aliasing — a bare decimation of a fine texture produces moiré, not a small picture. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">pyrUp</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">targetWidth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">width</span> <span class="o">&#42;</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">targetHeight</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">height</span> <span class="o">&#42;</span> <span class="mi">2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span></code> | One-octave upsample to exactly `targetWidth` x `targetHeight` (default 2x), bilinear then smoothed by `sigma` to suppress the interpolation grid. The approximate inverse of `pyrDown`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">gaussianPyramid</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">levels</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">4</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">minSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">8</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GaussianPyramid</span></code> | Build a [`GaussianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-gaussianpyramid) with at most `levels` octaves, stopping at `minSize` pixels. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">laplacianPyramid</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">levels</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">4</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">sigma</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">minSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">8</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">LaplacianPyramid</span></code> | Build a [`LaplacianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-laplacianpyramid): at each octave, `band = level - pyrUp(pyrDown(level))`. The reconstruction is exact up to the upsampling filter, so it is a genuine invertible band-splitting — the basis of multiband blending, texture synthesis and detail transfer. |

### Top-level values { #imaging-filters-kt-values }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">SOBEL&#95;DERIV</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Kernel1D</span></code> | The Sobel 3x3 derivative factor, **scaled to true units-per-pixel**: `[-1, 0, 1]/2`, i.e. the central difference `(f(x+1) - f(x-1)) / 2`. The classic unscaled `[-1, 0, 1]` reports twice the actual slope; dividing by 2 here means `sobel().dx` on a ramp of slope `s` really is `s`, and a unit step edge really does integrate to a total gradient of 1. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">SOBEL&#95;SMOOTH</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Kernel1D</span></code> | The Sobel smoothing factor, normalised. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">SCHARR&#95;SMOOTH</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Kernel1D</span></code> | The Scharr smoothing factor (`[3, 10, 3]/16`) — better rotational symmetry than Sobel's. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">LAPLACIAN&#95;4</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Kernel2D</span></code> | The 4-neighbour discrete Laplacian. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="nc">LAPLACIAN&#95;8</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Kernel2D</span></code> | The 8-neighbour discrete Laplacian. |

### LaplacianPyramid { #imaging-filters-kt-laplacianpyramid }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">LaplacianPyramid</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">bands</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">residual</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Img</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

A Laplacian pyramid: `bands` hold the band-pass detail at each octave and `residual` is the coarsest low-pass. `reconstruct` inverts the decomposition (to within the blur's precision), which is exactly the invariant the unit test checks.

| --- | --- |

## imaging_geometry.kt { #imaging-geometry-kt }

Geometry and motion for [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img): affine and perspective warps, homography estimation from point
correspondences (DLT + RANSAC), and pyramidal Lucas–Kanade optical flow.

This is the part of the imaging family that relates *two* pictures rather than transforming one.
The through-line is:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val pts   = a.goodFeaturesToTrack(120)                 // where is there anything to track?
val flow  = opticalFlowLK(a, b, pts)                   // where did each of those go?
val fit   = findHomographyRansac(flow.sourcePoints(), flow.targetPoints())
val warped = b.warpPerspective(fit.homography.inverse()) // undo the motion
```

The linear algebra is deliberately self-contained (a 9x9 Jacobi eigen-solver and a 6x6 Gaussian
elimination), because a 3x3 homography does not justify a dependency and the whole point of this
family is that it works headless in a box with nothing installed.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/imaging_geometry.kt`

**Used in:** [Imaging and computer vision](../imaging_examples.md)

### Homography { #imaging-geometry-kt-homography }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Homography</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">m</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

A 2-D projective transform (homography), a 3x3 matrix in row-major order, mapping `(x, y) -> ((m0 x + m1 y + m2)/(m6 x + m7 y + m8), (m3 x + m4 y + m5)/(m6 x + m7 y + m8))`.

## imaging_simd.kt { #imaging-simd-kt }

The SIMD span kernels the imaging filters are built out of.

### Why this file exists

The scalar filter layer reads every sample through `Img.get`, which per multiply-add costs a
range check, a channel clamp and a `when` over [`Border`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-border). That is correct and readable, and it is
also unvectorizable: C2 cannot hoist a branch whose outcome depends on the loop index out of the
inner loop, so a 3-tap Sobel pays three bounds-checked calls per sample.

The fix is not to make the accessor faster — it is to stop calling it in the interior. Because
[`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) stores samples interleaved (`data[(y * width + x) * channels + c]`), *both* passes of a
separable convolution address contiguous memory:

- **Vertical.** For a fixed output row, tap `t` reads the whole of source row `y + t - r`. The
  border decision is therefore *per row*, not per pixel: resolve the row index once and the
  entire row is a straight span. Every row takes the fast path.
- **Horizontal.** Adding `(t - r) * channels` to a flat index moves to the same channel of the
  pixel `t - r` columns over. So for a fixed tap the whole interior of a row is, again, a
  straight span — only the `r` columns at each end need the general accessor.

### The one primitive that matters: `stencil`

Both observations reduce a convolution — separable *or* dense — to the same shape: a destination
span is a weighted sum of `k` source spans at fixed element offsets. That is `stencil`, and it
keeps the running sum **in a vector register** across all taps, so `k` taps cost `k` reads and
**one** write.

The alternative — accumulate in memory, one `axpy` per tap — costs `k` reads *and* `k`
read-modify-writes. For the sigma-2 Gaussian used in the benchmark (`radius 8`, 17 taps) that is
17 write passes over the image where one would do, and it is why `stencil` rather than `axpy` is
the inner loop of everything here. `axpy` survives only for the handful of border rows where each
tap resolves to a *different*, border-dependent source row and there is no single offset to fold.

### On unrolling, which is not optional

`stencil` is a chain of `k` dependent FMAs into one accumulator. On Apple silicon an FMA has ~4
cycles of latency and can issue ~4 per cycle, so a single-accumulator 17-tap chain runs at
latency, not throughput — about 16x off peak. The main loop therefore keeps **four** independent
accumulators (four output chunks in flight), which converts the chain into something the machine
can pipeline, then falls back to one chunk at a time and finally to scalar for the tail. This is
the difference between "uses the Vector API" and "is fast".

### Decimation, without a gather

A pass that throws half its output away should not compute it. Halving *rows* is free (just skip
them), but halving *columns* makes the reads stride-2, which on NEON means a gather. `splitByPhase`
avoids it: output `x` reads source pixel `2x + s`, whose parity is fixed by the parity of `s`. So
even-offset taps only ever read even-indexed pixels and odd-offset taps only odd ones. Split the
row into its even and odd pixels once — into one scratch buffer, laid out even-half then odd-half,
so a single `stencil` call can address both — and every tap is unit-stride again. This is the
polyphase decomposition, and it is what makes `Img.pyrDown` a half-resolution filter rather than a
full-resolution one with a discard at the end.

### On FMA

These kernels use fused multiply-add: one rounding per tap instead of two. Results therefore
differ from the scalar reference in the last ulp — more accurate, not less, but not bit-identical.
`ImagingSimdTest` asserts agreement to `2e-6f`, which is four orders of magnitude above this.
